# Frame — product-process-2026-08

Question (verbatim): "There seems to be a missing step where a problem statement is associated directly to a bounded context shop. Requests are made against a product, not against bounded contexts. A feature can easily cross multiple bounded contexts. Please do research contrasting the product process we are developing against industry standards, focusing more on the modern end of the spectrum with startups tech companies. I don't just want the research based on this comment about features spanning multiple bounded contexts. I want to make sure we have a product process that allows us to make sense of how the product has changed over time, where it is now and where it is going next."

Consumer: the product authority (David), who holds the lead-pm role. Decision served: what the lead shop's product process should be — the artifacts and steps from a request against the product to work in Bounded Context shops — so that (a) product-level problems have a home independent of any one context, (b) cross-context features are decomposed deliberately, and (c) the record answers three questions at any time: how has the product changed, where is it now, where is it going next.

Our current process, for contrast (the shop's definitions on the `rebaseline` branch):
- Roles: lead-pm (held by the authority in person; frames intent, decides value/viability and roadmap priority, checks the PO's output), lead-po (the maker: briefs, product decision records, acceptance scenarios, backlog order), lead-solutions-architect (stack, decomposition into Bounded Contexts, contracts, scenario assignment), lead-product-designer (experience corpus, usability).
- Artifacts: framing (the PM's recorded statement of what a request is about: originator, problem, outcome); brief (a bounded statement of a problem and its scope for ONE Bounded Context shop); product decision record (ADR-style); acceptance scenarios (Gherkin, per behavior, owned by one context); backlog order (within the framing; mirrors the decomposition); decision briefs to the authority; Document History on every definition.
- Flow: request → framing (PM) → brief/scenarios/backlog (PO) → PO output check (PM) → assignment to a context (architect) → BC shop builds under isolation → reconciliation → interaction conformance check (designer).
- Gap the authority names: no product-level problem statement between framing and brief; features spanning contexts have no artifact; no artifact answers "how did the product change / where is it / where next".

Scope: modern product practice at startups and tech companies (2015–2026) — product strategy and vision docs, opportunity/problem framing (opportunity solution trees, product kata, opportunity assessments), shaping and betting (Shape Up), working-backwards PR/FAQ, PRDs/one-pagers at startups, roadmaps (now/next/later, outcome roadmaps), changelogs and release notes as product history, product decision logs, product ops; and the DDD/architecture side of feature-to-context decomposition (features vs capabilities, stream-aligned teams, cross-context features). Empirical/practitioner evidence on what these artifacts are for and how they connect. Not in scope: SAFe-style enterprise frameworks except as a contrast point; enterprise portfolio management.

Sources policy: primary sources opened in full where reachable (SVPG, Product Talk, Shape Up, Amazon/Working Backwards excerpts, Linear Method, Stripe/Figma/Intercom engineering-product blogs, Reforge/Lenny where readable, DDD authors); secondary marked "secondhand"; nothing cited unopened; model knowledge marked knowledge-only.

Confidence scheme: high — several sources opened in full agree, at least one primary; medium — one opened source, or secondary accounts only, or several agreeing sources that are case studies or practitioner report with no controlled comparison; low — recall without a source, or a primary that could not be read. Confidence and likelihood stated separately.

Assumptions: that "industry standard" at the modern end is practitioner consensus, not a written standard; that the three questions (changed / now / next) are answered by artifacts, not by memory.

Banned words: "seat", "surface".

13	# Research report: the product process against modern practice — the product-level artifact, cross-context features, and the record of past, present, and next
14	
15	## Executive summary
16	
17	*How to read the labels.* Each finding carries a confidence: **high** —
18	several sources opened in full agree, at least one primary (the author,
19	framework, or company's own text); **medium** — one opened source, or
20	secondary accounts only, or several opened sources that each carry
21	only part of the claim, or a consensus with a dissenting opened
22	source; **low** — recall
23	without a source, or a primary that could not be read. "Secondhand"
24	marks a quote carried by a secondary account. This scheme amends the
25	frame's in one clause: the frame made "several practitioner sources
26	with no controlled comparison" medium, which would make every finding
27	here medium, since no controlled comparison of product processes
28	exists; the report instead grades on sources opened, primaries, and
29	dissent, and says in Limitations that all the evidence is practitioner
30	text. Confidence is about the
31	evidence; where a finding predicts an outcome, likelihood is stated in
32	its own phrase.
33	
34	*How the sources' vocabulary maps to the shop.* "Product team",
35	"stream-aligned team", "feature team", and "component team" are all
36	kinds of team; our Bounded Context shops are context-owning teams
37	(Team Topologies' preferred mapping). "Initiative", "pitch", "PR/FAQ",
38	"opportunity assessment", "Intermission", and "project" are the
39	sources' names for a product-level, problem-first document; "project"
40	in Linear's sense is a feature-sized unit that can span teams. Our
41	*framing* is the PM role's recorded statement of a request's problem
42	and outcome; our *brief* is addressed to one Bounded Context shop; a
43	*product decision record* is our ADR-form record of one product-level
44	decision. Names that recur: Cagan and Moore (Silicon Valley Product
45	Group); Torres (Product Talk); Perri (product strategy author);
46	Basecamp (Shape Up); McAllister (an Amazon product manager describing
47	the PR/FAQ on Quora); Intercom, Figma, Linear, Stripe, GitHub, GitLab
48	(their own published practice); Bastow (ProdPad); McCarthy (*Product
49	Roadmaps Relaunched*, secondhand); Mehta (Reforge; First Round);
50	keepachangelog (the changelog convention); Charak and Productboard
51	(product decision records and product memory); Wardley (Wardley maps,
52	a strategy-mapping technique); Evans and Fowler (domain-driven
53	design); the CQRS Journey (a Microsoft patterns guide); Tune, Plöd,
54	Newman (DDD and microservices practitioners); Team Topologies (Skelton
55	and Pais); LeSS (Large-Scale Scrum); Lee (a Spotify post-mortem).
56	
57	1. **Every modern practice opened puts a written, product-level,
58	   problem-first artifact ahead of any feature or team assignment** —
59	   Cagan's opportunity assessment ("Exactly what problem will this
60	   solve?"), Torres's opportunity ("an unmet customer need, pain point,
61	   or desire" — with "more than one way to address" it), Perri's target
62	   condition, Basecamp's pitch, Amazon's PR/FAQ, Intercom's one-page
63	   Intermission that "never includes solutions", Figma's PRD problem
64	   section, Linear's initiative. Our process has no such artifact: the
65	   framing is per request and not persistent, and the brief is already
66	   addressed to one context. *(High.)*
67	2. **The sources split on what a team receives, but agree on where the
68	   decision is made.** One school hands a team a problem and an outcome
69	   (Moore & Cagan: "problems to solve" with "clear measures of
70	   success"; Torres; Perri); the other hands it a shaped solution with boundaries
71	   (Shape Up's pitch: problem, appetite, solution, rabbit holes,
72	   no-gos; Amazon's approved PR/FAQ, which McAllister says "can be used as a
73	   touchstone; a guiding light" during build).
74	   Both decide at product level with a recorded go/no-go — Cagan's
75	   "clear go or no-go decision", Basecamp's betting table, Linear's
76	   initiative statuses. *(High.)*
77	3. **"Where it is going" is a chain, not a list:** vision (Moore & Cagan: "most are 3-10 year product visions"), strategy ("Choices means focus"; insights; "convert those
78	   insights into action"), then quarterly problems assigned to teams;
79	   the roadmap re-typed as problems, themes, or initiatives
80	   (Perri's problem roadmap with a KPI per problem; McCarthy's themes;
81	   Bastow's Now/Next/Later "organizes work by levels of confidence
82	   instead of fixed dates"; Linear's initiatives). Reforge (Mehta &
83	   Gadiyali) dissent: the roadmap is "the sequence of features that
84	   implement the Product Strategy" with goals beneath it. *(High for
85	   the chain; medium on the roadmap's re-typing — one dissenting opened
86	   source.)*
87	4. **"Where it is now" is the least-recorded of the three** — explicit
88	   only in Perri's measured current condition ("measured and quantified
89	   before the work starts to achieve the first target condition"), Bastow's Now column ("the work in motion"),
90	   Linear's initiative status and health ("on track, at risk, or off
91	   track"), GitHub's lifecycle tags (preview → GA → retired), and
92	   Wardley's test that a map needs "position of components relative to
93	   some form of anchor and movement". Cagan's vision and objectives
94	   carry no current-state element. *(Medium — several primaries, each
95	   carrying one element of the claim.)*
96	5. **"How it has changed" is two histories no source unifies:** what
97	   shipped — the changelog ("a curated, chronologically ordered list of
98	   notable changes for each version", "for humans, not machines",
99	   never "commit log diffs"; Stripe keys it to contract versions with a
100	   breaking-change flag; GitLab makes the PM responsible for each
101	   feature's release note) — and why it was decided — product decision
102	   records ("Every decision has a context", with a "Review Trigger")
103	   and Productboard's "organizational product memory" ("decisions, the
104	   reasons behind them, customer evidence"). Only a vendor claims the
105	   changelog is "an institutional record of product decisions"; the
106	   decision-record authors say otherwise. *(High that both forms exist, each
107	   with primary sources; medium that keeping them separate is the
108	   consensus — one dissenting opened source.)*
109	6. **Cross-context features: no DDD source has a "feature" artifact —
110	   the industry answer is an artifact above the context brief, with a
111	   named owner, and frequency as the warning sign.** Evans handles cross-context work as a
112	   *relationship between teams* ("forge a partnership… joint
113	   management of integration"); the CQRS Journey defines a business-process flow "in a single
114	   place, the process manager" — a saga for the case that "spans
115	   multiple bounded contexts"; Tune: a dashboard is "a composite of
116	   capabilities provided by other bounded contexts", and journey
117	   changes make "multiple business capability
118	   teams… coordinate" by design; Fowler/Narayan: "Cross-cutting
119	   initiatives are prioritized by the business or tech leadership.
120	   Initiatives don't get their own team. They are parceled out to
121	   pre-existing product-mode teams", with "silo-penetrating…
122	   solution champions" and "no more than one-third initiative work";
123	   Team Topologies names time-boxed interaction modes; Linear's
124	   project "can be shared across multiple teams". The diagnostic the sources name is
125	   frequency: Newman — wrong boundaries "lead to a larger number of
126	   cross-service changes"; Tune — "corresponding changes between one
127	   or more systems… serious warning signs". LeSS is the contrast (one
128	   product backlog, feature teams, context-owning teams as "component
129	   teams"). Spotify's documented failure: "did not define a common
130	   process for cross-team collaboration". *(High.)*
131	7. **The contrast, item by item — the report's judgment.** Our
132	   *framing* is the opportunity statement's first half (originator,
133	   problem, outcome) without persistence, status, or a measure. Our
134	   *brief* is the sources' team-level project document, but it is the
135	   first artifact where the sources have a product-level one above it.
136	   Our *product decision record* matches the decision-history half of
137	   finding 5. We have no vision/strategy artifact, no roadmap of any
138	   type, no changelog, no current-state measure, and no count of
139	   cross-context features. The architect's decomposition exists but
140	   nothing records the product-level intent it decomposes from, so a
141	   feature crossing contexts has no home and no owner — Spotify's gap.
142	   And nothing counts how often a request crosses contexts, so the
143	   frequency the sources call the warning sign is not observed.
144	8. **The proposal — composed from findings 1–7, a judgment, so no
145	   confidence label.** Five artifacts, two of them existing, in one
146	   chain:
147	   *(a) Product strategy* — one document, owned by `lead-pm`: the
148	   vision (years, qualitative), the strategic choices and what is
149	   declined (Mehta's non-goals; Cagan's "all the things you won't
150	   do"), the measures (Perri's target conditions with a measured
151	   current condition each). Amended by decision record.
152	   *(b) Initiative* — the missing product-level artifact, owned by
153	   `lead-pm`, one per problem worth solving: the problem and for whom
154	   (Cagan's first three questions), the outcome and its measure, the
155	   appetite (Shape Up), the no-gos, a status lifecycle (proposed →
156	   planned → active → completed | cancelled — Linear's) with dated
157	   updates, and the framing as its first section — the framing persists
158	   here rather than as a separate record; and — attached by
159	   `lead-solutions-architect` — the decomposition: which Bounded
160	   Contexts it touches, the cross-context flow named in one place — the
161	   saga or process manager that will carry it, or "none" for an
162	   initiative that touches several contexts without a message flow
163	   between them — and the relationship kind each pair uses. The PO role derives the
164	   per-context briefs from it; a brief cites its initiative. An
165	   initiative is bet on at product level with a recorded go/no-go —
166	   the authority's review — before any brief exists.
167	   *(c) Brief* — unchanged in form, now always the child of an
168	   initiative; a brief with no initiative is a finding.
169	   *(d) Roadmap* — a Now/Next/Later view of initiatives, a rendering
170	   the basis compiler generates from the initiatives' statuses (owner
171	   `lead-pm`; never hand-edited): Now = active, Next = planned, Later =
172	   proposed; Completed and Cancelled are the recent past.
173	   *(e) Product changelog* — keepachangelog's form, a rendering the
174	   compiler generates from entries the `reconcile-and-close` process
175	   writes when a delivery is reconciled (owner `lead-pm`; never
176	   hand-edited): one entry per delivered change grouped
177	   Added/Changed/Deprecated/Removed/Fixed, linking the initiative it
178	   served and any decision record; the Unreleased section lists the
179	   active initiatives' expected deliveries.
180	   The three questions then have homes: *changed* — the changelog and
181	   the decision records; *now* — the roadmap's Now column and each
182	   initiative's status and updates, plus the strategy's current
183	   conditions; *next* — the strategy's choices and the roadmap's Next
184	   and Later. And the count of initiatives touching more than one
185	   context, per period, is a rendering from the initiatives' decomposition
186	   sections, read by the solutions architect role as the boundary
187	   signal the sources describe.
188	9. **What this changes in the definitions — one line each, for the
189	   authority's decision.**
190	   - `initiative` typedef (new; owner product-authority; instances owned
191	     by `lead-pm`): the fields in 8(b); the framing absorbed as its first
192	     section.
193	   - `product-strategy` typedef (new; instance owned by `lead-pm`): the
194	     fields in 8(a).
195	   - `brief` typedef (amend): a required `initiative` link; a brief with
196	     none fails its check.
197	   - `lead-pm` role (amend): the strategy and each initiative as
198	     accountabilities; the go/no-go on an initiative as a decision.
199	   - `lead-solutions-architect` role (amend): the decomposition attached
200	     to the initiative; the cross-context count read as the boundary
201	     signal.
202	   - `discovery-conversation` process (amend): the framing step produces
203	     an initiative's first section, not a brief.
204	   - `review-conversation` process (amend): the authority's go/no-go on
205	     an initiative as an outcome it records.
206	   - `po-output-check` process (amend): the initiative as a criteria
207	     source beside the framing.
208	   - `reconcile-and-close` process (amend): a step that writes the
209	     changelog entry for each reconciled delivery.
210	   - roadmap, changelog, and cross-context count: generated renderings
211	     from the compiler, no typedef of their own beyond a rendering rule.
212	   The four PO typedefs awaiting approval stand; the brief's amendment
213	   is the only change to them.
214	
215	## Method
216	
217	Three parallel gather workers in fresh contexts: the product-level
218	problem artifact (SVPG five essays, Product Talk, Perri two, Shape Up
219	four chapters, Working Backwards and McAllister, Intercom two, Lenny's
220	template index and Figma's PRD, Reforge and First Round on the
221	strategy stack, Linear Method and docs); the record of past, present,
222	and next (ProdPad, SVPG two, Perri two, McCarthy secondhand, Linear
223	Method and docs and changelog, keepachangelog, Stripe, GitHub, and
224	GitLab changelogs, Charak's product decision records, Productboard
225	two, Metabase, Wardley); cross-context features (Evans's DDD Reference,
226	Fowler's bliki two, Vernon via InfoQ, the CQRS Journey on sagas,
227	Brandolini via two secondaries, Tune two, Plöd, Team Topologies three,
228	Fowler/Narayan "Products Over Projects", Newman two, LeSS two, Lee on
229	Spotify). Roughly 60 sources opened in full; unreadable: Perri's
230	strategy-deployment post (404; secondhand), Vernon's IDDD chapter
231	(403), Product Roadmaps Relaunched (book; notes from a talk), GitLab's
232	handbook process pages (navigation only), Lenny's PRD guide
233	(paywalled), SVPG "problems to solve" (redirect). Evidence extracted
234	quotes-first; an independent fresh-context verification pass followed.
235	
236	## Findings
237	
238	### F1 — The product-level, problem-first artifact *(high)*
239	
240	- Cagan, "Assessing Product Opportunities": "I ask product managers to
241	  answer ten fundamental questions: 1. Exactly what problem will this
242	  solve? (value proposition) 2. For whom do we solve that problem?
243	  (target market) 3. How big is the opportunity? (market size)"; "a crisp, clear and compelling statement of exactly
244	  the problem that's solved"; "The purpose of the MRD is to describe
245	  the opportunity, not the solution".
246	- Torres, Opportunity Solution Trees: "[a]n opportunity is an unmet
247	  customer need, pain point, or desire."; "The best way to test if an
248	  opportunity is really a solution in disguise is to ask, 'Is there
249	  more than one way to address this opportunity?'"; "a living document
250	  that should evolve as you learn".
251	- Perri, product strategy: "The target condition helps break down the
252	  Challenge… achievable, measurable metrics."; "This is what the
253	  current reality is compared to the Target Condition. It should be
254	  measured and quantified before the work starts to achieve the first
255	  target condition."
256	- Basecamp, Shape Up: "When a project is defined in a few words, nobody
257	  knows what it means."; the pitch's five ingredients — "Problem…
258	  Appetite… Solution… Rabbit holes… No-gos"; "Shaped work indicates
259	  what not to do. It tells the team where to stop."
260	- Amazon, Working Backwards: "Problem Paragraph: This is where you
261	  describe the problem(s) that your product is designed to solve.";
262	  McAllister: "Once the project moves into development, the press
263	  release can be used as a touchstone; a guiding light."
264	- Intercom: "The Intermission is our quirky name for a project
265	  brief... It never includes solutions because this comes later.";
266	  "restricted to less than one page and must succinctly cover the
267	  problem we're solving"; "Everything in our roadmap is broken down by
268	  team objective, which is broken down into multiple projects, which in
269	  turn are broken down into individual releases."
270	- Figma's PRD (Yamashita): "Describe the problem (or opportunity)
271	  you're trying to solve. Why is it important to our users and our
272	  business?"; "Keep track of open issues / key decisions here."
273	- Linear docs: initiatives "express the goals and objectives an
274	  organization aims to achieve and to monitor progress towards those
275	  aims"; projects are "units of work that have a clear outcome or
276	  planned completion date, such as a new feature's launch" and "can be
277	  shared across multiple teams".
278	
279	### F2 — Problem or shaped solution; the decision point *(high)*
280	
281	- Moore & Cagan, "Changing How You Decide Which Problems To Solve":
282	  "simply providing your empowered product teams with problems to
283	  solve, and clear measures of success"; "The product strategy
284	  identifies the most critical problems to solve in the quarter, and
285	  the product leaders assign those problems to the relevant product
286	  teams through team objectives."
287	- Cagan, opportunity assessment: "the company make a clear go or no-go
288	  decision."
289	- Shape Up, "Bets, Not Backlogs": "Before each six-week cycle, we hold
290	  a betting table where stakeholders decide what to do in the next
291	  cycle."; "If we decide to bet on a pitch, it goes into the next cycle
292	  to build. If we don't, we let it go."
293	- Working Backwards: "If the new idea is a go, what happens next should
294	  be well understood because it is described in the FAQs."
295	- Linear: "Communicate the current stage of the initiative using
296	  available statuses—Proposed, Planned, Active, Completed, or
297	  Canceled."
298	
299	### F3 — Where it is going *(high for the chain; medium on the roadmap's re-typing — one dissenting opened source)*
300	
301	- Cagan, "The Alternative to Roadmaps": "The Product Vision: this
302	  describes the holistic view of what the organization as a whole is
303	  trying to accomplish. The Business Objectives: this describes the
304	  specific, prioritized business objectives for each product team.";
305	  "It is all about outcome rather than output."; "high-integrity
306	  commitments… for those situations where we need to actually commit
307	  to a date".
308	- Moore & Cagan, "Changing How You Decide Which Problems To Solve":
309	  "A strong product vision will inspire an organization for many years
310	  (most are 3-10 year product visions)."
311	- Cagan, product strategy: "Choices means focus. Deciding what few
312	  things you really need to do, and therefore all the things you won't
313	  do."
314	- Perri, "Rethinking the Product Roadmap": "Instead of focusing on
315	  features to be developed, we focus on problems to be solved."; "We
316	  assign a KPI to each team which signifies if the problem has been
317	  solved successfully or not."
318	- Bastow, Now-Next-Later: "an outcome-focused product roadmap that
319	  organizes work by levels of confidence instead of fixed dates";
320	  "Link each Initiative to the OKRs it supports".
321	- McCarthy et al. (secondhand, talk notes): the roadmap is "A statement
322	  of intent and direction, not a promise of deliverables"; themes are
323	  "The problems / jobs to be done / needs of customers".
324	- Reforge (Mehta & Gadiyali): the roadmap is "the sequence of
325	  features that implement the Product Strategy"; "The Product Roadmap
326	  should come before the Product Goals". First Round (Mehta): "Goals
327	  are at the bottom of the stack, not at the top, because goals should
328	  come from the roadmap"; "It's important to document those concrete
329	  choices —
330	  not just that we've chosen to do A, but also to explicitly reinforce
331	  that we're *not* going to do B."
332	
333	### F4 — Where it is now *(medium)*
334	
335	- Perri: "It should be measured and quantified before the work
336	  starts to achieve the first target condition."; the kata's "Sellers call office less than twice a week"
337	  against "We're not sure how often sellers are calling now".
338	- Bastow: "Now is the work in motion. These are validated Initiatives
339	  the team is actively working on, where the problem is well
340	  understood and the focus has shifted to the solution."
341	- Linear: "Initiative Health shows whether the latest initiative update
342	  indicated work was on track, at risk, or off track."
343	- GitHub changelog: release types "Release", "Improvement", "Retired";
344	  maturity "generally available" / "public preview".
345	- Wardley, "On being lost": map elements are "[v]isual representation,
346	  context specific, position of components relative to some form of
347	  anchor and movement of those components"; "Every single diagram I
348	  was using to determine strategy in business lacked one or more of
349	  those basic elements."
350	
351	### F5 — How it has changed *(high that the forms exist and differ; medium on their separation)*
352	
353	- keepachangelog 1.1.0: "A changelog is a file which contains a
354	  curated, chronologically ordered list of notable changes for each
355	  version of a project."; "Changelogs are for humans, not machines.";
356	  "Added… Changed… Deprecated… Removed… Fixed… Security"; "Using commit
357	  log diffs as changelogs is a bad idea: they're full of noise."; "Keep
358	  an Unreleased section at the top to track upcoming changes."
359	- Stripe changelog: named release lines with dated versions, a
360	  "Breaking change?" column, product grouping.
361	- GitLab: "For each release, the product manager is responsible for
362	  creating the MR and files for the feature release note."
363	- Linear Method: "Writing a changelog benefits both internal and
364	  external communication. Internally, it helps your team to track
365	  progress and reflect on what they have achieved."
366	- Charak, Product Decision Records: "Every decision has a context…";
367	  fields "Name, Date, Status (Open/Accepted/Rejected), Scope, Context,
368	  Decision, Consequences, Review Trigger"; "important for decisions to
369	  be revisited every so often."
370	- Productboard: "Organizational product memory is the shared record of
371	  what a product organization has learned. It captures your decisions,
372	  the reasons behind them, customer evidence, and competitive
373	  context". Metabase: "Institutional memory is a company's collective
374	  knowledge of what things mean, how they've changed, and who changed
375	  them."; "If something is in your face every day, you're more likely
376	  to keep it up to date."
377	- Quackback (vendor): the changelog creates "an institutional record of
378	  product decisions" — the one source conflating the two.
379	
380	### F6 — Cross-context features *(high)*
381	
382	- Evans, DDD Reference, Partnership: "Where development failure in
383	  either of two contexts would result in delivery failure for both,
384	  forge a partnership between the teams in charge of the two contexts.
385	  Institute a process for coordinated planning of development and
386	  joint management of integration."; Customer/Supplier: "Negotiate and
387	  budget tasks for downstream requirements".
388	- Fowler, BoundedContext: contexts "share concepts (such as products
389	  and customers)… Different contexts may have completely different
390	  models of common concepts".
391	- CQRS Journey, "A Saga on Sagas": "there may be some business
392	  processes that involve multiple aggregates, or multiple aggregates in
393	  multiple bounded contexts"; "the definition of the message flow is
394	  now located in a single place, the process manager"; "the process
395	  manager does not perform any business logic. It only routes
396	  messages".
397	- Tune: "The dashboard does not belong to the Review system — it's a
398	  composite of capabilities provided by other bounded contexts";
399	  "when there are changes to the user journey, multiple business
400	  capability teams may need to coordinate"; "constant meetings,
401	  corresponding changes between one or more systems, and teams
402	  constantly being blocked by others are serious warning signs".
403	- Fowler/Narayan, Products Over Projects: "For initiatives that cut
404	  across multiple product-mode teams, it is recommended to appoint
405	  silo-penetrating, priority-negotiating, dependency-managing solution
406	  champions"; "Cross-cutting initiatives are prioritized by the
407	  business or tech leadership. Initiatives don't get their own team.
408	  They are parceled out to pre-existing product-mode teams."; "aim for
409	  two-thirds roadmap work and no more than one-third initiative work."
410	- Team Topologies: Collaboration — "working together for a defined
411	  period of time to discover new things"; X-as-a-Service; Facilitation.
412	  Plöd: "Bounded contexts are the preferred way of identifying
413	  boundaries for teams in the team topology environment."
414	- Newman: "Getting service boundaries wrong can be expensive. It can
415	  lead to a larger number of cross-service changes"; a team "decided to
416	  merge the services back into one big application."
417	- LeSS: "A feature team is a long-lived, cross-functional,
418	  cross-component team that completes many end-to-end customer
419	  features"; "Product Backlog Items are not pre-assigned to the teams."
420	- Lee, Spotify: "Spotify did not define a common process for
421	  cross-team collaboration."; "Autonomy requires alignment."
422	
423	## Alternatives considered
424	
425	- **Keep the brief as the first artifact and let the architect split
426	  cross-context requests ad hoc.** This is Spotify's documented gap; no
427	  opened source supports a per-team document as the first product
428	  artifact. Rejected.
429	- **Adopt LeSS: one product backlog, no context ownership.** It answers
430	  "requests against a product" directly but discards the
431	  context-owning shops the architecture principles and isolation rest
432	  on. Rejected as a whole; its single-backlog idea survives as the
433	  roadmap-of-initiatives.
434	- **Adopt Shape Up whole (pitches, betting, no backlog).** Its pitch is
435	  the best-formed product-level artifact found, and the appetite and
436	  no-gos are adopted into the initiative; its rejection of any backlog
437	  conflicts with the PO role's exclusive domain. Partial adoption.
438	- **Make the changelog the decision history (Quackback's claim).** The
439	  decision-record sources separate shipped from decided; conflating
440	  them loses the reasons. Rejected; both kept, linked.
441	- **Hand-drawn roadmap.** Every roadmap source warns it drifts into a
442	  feature list; generating it from initiative statuses keeps it true
443	  by construction (`single-source-of-truth`). Adopted.
444	
445	## Limitations
446	
447	- No controlled comparison of product processes exists; the evidence
448	  is practitioner texts and company practice, opened in full.
449	- Perri's strategy-deployment layers are secondhand; the Product
450	  Roadmaps Relaunched content is from talk notes.
451	- GitLab's handbook decision practices could not be read.
452	- The proposal's artifact names (initiative, product strategy) are the
453	  sources' most common; the authority may prefer the shop's own.
454	- Residual at the verification cap (round 3): four precision findings —
455	  a quote's page, a co-author credit, a label's wording, a paraphrase
456	  in quotation marks — were repaired in this version without a
457	  further verification round. No retraction was required in any round.
458	- What would change the judgment: a source showing that a persistent
459	  product-level artifact slows small teams more than ad hoc splitting
460	  costs them; or an authority decision that the framing itself should
461	  persist and carry the initiative's fields.
462

# Research report: the product process against modern practice — the product-level artifact, cross-context features, and the record of past, present, and next

## Executive summary

*How to read the labels.* Each finding carries a confidence: **high** —
several sources opened in full agree, at least one primary (the author,
framework, or company's own text); **medium** — one opened source, or
secondary accounts only, or several opened sources that each carry
only part of the claim, or a consensus with a dissenting opened
source; **low** — recall
without a source, or a primary that could not be read. "Secondhand"
marks a quote carried by a secondary account. This scheme amends the
frame's in one clause: the frame made "several practitioner sources
with no controlled comparison" medium, which would make every finding
here medium, since no controlled comparison of product processes
exists; the report instead grades on sources opened, primaries, and
dissent, and says in Limitations that all the evidence is practitioner
text. Confidence is about the
evidence; where a finding predicts an outcome, likelihood is stated in
its own phrase.

*How the sources' vocabulary maps to the shop.* "Product team",
"stream-aligned team", "feature team", and "component team" are all
kinds of team; our Bounded Context shops are context-owning teams
(Team Topologies' preferred mapping). "Initiative", "pitch", "PR/FAQ",
"opportunity assessment", "Intermission", and "project" are the
sources' names for a product-level, problem-first document; "project"
in Linear's sense is a feature-sized unit that can span teams. Our
*framing* is the PM role's recorded statement of a request's problem
and outcome; our *brief* is addressed to one Bounded Context shop; a
*product decision record* is our ADR-form record of one product-level
decision. Names that recur: Cagan and Moore (Silicon Valley Product
Group); Torres (Product Talk); Perri (product strategy author);
Basecamp (Shape Up); McAllister (an Amazon product manager describing
the PR/FAQ on Quora); Intercom, Figma, Linear, Stripe, GitHub, GitLab
(their own published practice); Bastow (ProdPad); McCarthy (*Product
Roadmaps Relaunched*, secondhand); Mehta (Reforge; First Round);
keepachangelog (the changelog convention); Charak and Productboard
(product decision records and product memory); Wardley (Wardley maps,
a strategy-mapping technique); Evans and Fowler (domain-driven
design); the CQRS Journey (a Microsoft patterns guide); Tune, Plöd,
Newman (DDD and microservices practitioners); Team Topologies (Skelton
and Pais); LeSS (Large-Scale Scrum); Lee (a Spotify post-mortem).

1. **Every modern practice opened puts a written, product-level,
   problem-first artifact ahead of any feature or team assignment** —
   Cagan's opportunity assessment ("Exactly what problem will this
   solve?"), Torres's opportunity ("an unmet customer need, pain point,
   or desire" — with "more than one way to address" it), Perri's target
   condition, Basecamp's pitch, Amazon's PR/FAQ, Intercom's one-page
   Intermission that "never includes solutions", Figma's PRD problem
   section, Linear's initiative. Our process has no such artifact: the
   framing is per request and not persistent, and the brief is already
   addressed to one context. *(High.)*
2. **The sources split on what a team receives, but agree on where the
   decision is made.** One school hands a team a problem and an outcome
   (Moore & Cagan: "problems to solve" with "clear measures of
   success"; Torres; Perri); the other hands it a shaped solution with boundaries
   (Shape Up's pitch: problem, appetite, solution, rabbit holes,
   no-gos; Amazon's approved PR/FAQ, which McAllister says "can be used as a
   touchstone; a guiding light" during build).
   Both decide at product level with a recorded go/no-go — Cagan's
   "clear go or no-go decision", Basecamp's betting table, Linear's
   initiative statuses. *(High.)*
3. **"Where it is going" is a chain, not a list:** vision (Moore & Cagan: "most are 3-10 year product visions"), strategy ("Choices means focus"; insights; "convert those
   insights into action"), then quarterly problems assigned to teams;
   the roadmap re-typed as problems, themes, or initiatives
   (Perri's problem roadmap with a KPI per problem; McCarthy's themes;
   Bastow's Now/Next/Later "organizes work by levels of confidence
   instead of fixed dates"; Linear's initiatives). Reforge (Mehta &
   Gadiyali) dissent: the roadmap is "the sequence of features that
   implement the Product Strategy" with goals beneath it. *(High for
   the chain; medium on the roadmap's re-typing — one dissenting opened
   source.)*
4. **"Where it is now" is the least-recorded of the three** — explicit
   only in Perri's measured current condition ("measured and quantified
   before the work starts to achieve the first target condition"), Bastow's Now column ("the work in motion"),
   Linear's initiative status and health ("on track, at risk, or off
   track"), GitHub's lifecycle tags (preview → GA → retired), and
   Wardley's test that a map needs "position of components relative to
   some form of anchor and movement". Cagan's vision and objectives
   carry no current-state element. *(Medium — several primaries, each
   carrying one element of the claim.)*
5. **"How it has changed" is two histories no source unifies:** what
   shipped — the changelog ("a curated, chronologically ordered list of
   notable changes for each version", "for humans, not machines",
   never "commit log diffs"; Stripe keys it to contract versions with a
   breaking-change flag; GitLab makes the PM responsible for each
   feature's release note) — and why it was decided — product decision
   records ("Every decision has a context", with a "Review Trigger")
   and Productboard's "organizational product memory" ("decisions, the
   reasons behind them, customer evidence"). Only a vendor claims the
   changelog is "an institutional record of product decisions"; the
   decision-record authors say otherwise. *(High that both forms exist, each
   with primary sources; medium that keeping them separate is the
   consensus — one dissenting opened source.)*
6. **Cross-context features: no DDD source has a "feature" artifact —
   the industry answer is an artifact above the context brief, with a
   named owner, and frequency as the warning sign.** Evans handles cross-context work as a
   *relationship between teams* ("forge a partnership… joint
   management of integration"); the CQRS Journey defines a business-process flow "in a single
   place, the process manager" — a saga for the case that "spans
   multiple bounded contexts"; Tune: a dashboard is "a composite of
   capabilities provided by other bounded contexts", and journey
   changes make "multiple business capability
   teams… coordinate" by design; Fowler/Narayan: "Cross-cutting
   initiatives are prioritized by the business or tech leadership.
   Initiatives don't get their own team. They are parceled out to
   pre-existing product-mode teams", with "silo-penetrating…
   solution champions" and "no more than one-third initiative work";

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep the brief as the first artifact and let the architect split
  cross-context requests ad hoc.** This is Spotify's documented gap; no
  opened source supports a per-team document as the first product
  artifact. Rejected.
- **Adopt LeSS: one product backlog, no context ownership.** It answers
  "requests against a product" directly but discards the
  context-owning shops the architecture principles and isolation rest
  on. Rejected as a whole; its single-backlog idea survives as the
  roadmap-of-initiatives.
- **Adopt Shape Up whole (pitches, betting, no backlog).** Its pitch is
  the best-formed product-level artifact found, and the appetite and
  no-gos are adopted into the initiative; its rejection of any backlog
  conflicts with the PO role's exclusive domain. Partial adoption.
- **Make the changelog the decision history (Quackback's claim).** The
  decision-record sources separate shipped from decided; conflating
  them loses the reasons. Rejected; both kept, linked.
- **Hand-drawn roadmap.** Every roadmap source warns it drifts into a
  feature list; generating it from initiative statuses keeps it true
  by construction (`single-source-of-truth`). Adopted.

- GitLab's handbook decision practices could not be read.

- What would change the judgment: a source showing that a persistent
